title: Sound
introductionText:
Physics
Sound
The Big Idea: Every sound comes from something — we call that thing a source of sound. We hear sounds with our ears. And a sound gets
fainter and fainter the further you go away from it.
Say It Like This
Read aloud
"Close your eyes and listen. What can you hear? A car outside? A bird? The fan? Every one of those sounds came from something. That
something is called a source of sound. The lion roars, the clock ticks, the bell rings — and your ears catch all of it."
Different instruments, different actions
You hit it triangle, cymbals
You shake it maracas, tambourine
You blow it trumpet, whistle
You pluck it sitar, oud, guitar
You beat it drum
triangle maracas trumpet sitar drum
HIT SHAKE BLOW PLUCK BEAT
Five instruments, five different actions. Which ones can you make from a box and a rubber band?
Try It at Home
Activity 1 — Sound boxes
Take three small empty boxes or plastic containers. Put rice in the first, a stone or a coin in the second, cotton wool or a feather in the
third. Close them and shake each one. Ask: "Which is loud? Which is quiet? Why do you think?" Hard, heavy things make loud sounds.
Soft, light things make almost none.
Activity 2 — How far can you hear it?
Stand in one place and bang a pot with a wooden spoon. He walks away one step at a time, counting his steps, until he cannot hear it any
more. Write the number down. Now bang the pot harder and repeat. He can walk further this time.
Two lessons in one game: a louder sound travels further, and every sound gets fainter with distance.
drum 20 steps away
loud quieter fainter and fainter
The further the sound travels, the fainter it gets — until the ear cannot catch it.
More examples to talk about
Name the source: the doorbell, the call to prayer, a car horn, the kettle whistling, a baby crying, the fan, rain on the window, your own
voice (your throat is a source of sound!).
Loud or quiet? A whisper, a shout, a pin dropping, a door slamming, a cat's paws, thunder. Sort them from quietest to loudest on a line
drawn on paper.
Feel the sound: put his hand gently on his throat and ask him to hum. He can feel the buzzing. Do the same on a drum skin while it is
beaten. Sound and shaking go together.
Key Words
sound source of sound loud quiet fainter ears hit shake blow pluck

sourceQuestions.sourceText: Which part of your body do you use to hear?

Write the action you use to make a sound with each instrument. Use: hit, shake, blow, pluck, beat
a) triangle b) maracas
c) trumpet d) sitar e) drum
sourceQuestions.answerKeyText: a) hit b) shake c) blow d) pluck e) beat

sourceQuestions.sourceText: Two boxes are shaken. One has a stone inside, one has a feather inside. Which one makes the louder sound? stone / feather
sourceQuestions.answerKeyText: The stone — it is hard and heavy, so it makes a much louder sound than a feather.

sourceQuestions.sourceText: Complete the sentence: As you walk away from a drum, the sound gets and .
sourceQuestions.answerKeyText: quieter and fainter (accept: softer, harder to hear)

sourceQuestions.sourceText:
Four children walked away from a drum until they could not hear it. Annay stopped at 20 steps, Zara at 14, Maris at 23, David at 8.
a) Who could hear the drum from the furthest away?
b) How many steps did Maris take?
How could you make a louder sound with two tapping sticks?
sourceQuestions.answerKeyText: Tap them together harder. (A bigger push makes a louder sound.)

sourceQuestions.sourceText: Put these in order from the quietest to the loudest:thunder, a whisper, a door slamming, a cat walking
sourceQuestions.answerKeyText: A cat walking → a whisper → a door slamming → thunder.

sourceQuestions.sourceText: Put your hand on your throat and hum. What can you feel?
sourceQuestions.answerKeyText: A buzzing or shaking under his hand. Sound is made by something shaking very fast.

As you walk away, a sound becomes ( louder ) ( fainter )
